props.title: Prey for Rock & Roll

sections.content: Prey for Rock & Roll (2003) captures the gritty reality of aging rockers in LA's underground music scene, with Gina Gershon delivering a raw performance as Jacki, a tattooed rocker approaching 40 and questioning her lifelong dedication to music. The film joins a powerful lineage of women-in-rock narratives like Ladies and Gentlemen, The Fabulous Stains (1982) and The Runaways (2010), but uniquely focuses on the struggle to maintain artistic passion well past youth. Director Alex Steyermark brings authentic punk energy, drawing from his music supervision work on films like Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001).

sections.content: The film stands out for addressing rarely-explored territory in rock movies - the working-class reality of career musicians who never "made it big." Like CBGB (2013) and What We Do Is Secret (2007), it strips away glamorous myths about the punk scene to show the daily grind. Gershon's character teaches guitar lessons, works day jobs, and plays small clubs - a stark contrast to rise-and-fall narratives like The Rose (1979) or Almost Famous (2000).

The authentic portrayal of women in rock sets it apart, showing complex relationships between bandmates while avoiding typical music film clichés. Like 20 Feet from Stardom (2013) and The Other F Word (2011), it explores how gender and age impact musicians' experiences. The film's unflinching look at sexual assault, addiction, and death in the music scene echoes darker rock documentaries like Dig! (2004). SUBHEAD: Women Behind the Music

sections.content: While many rock films focus on male musicians' perspectives, Prey for Rock & Roll joins films like Satisfaction (1988) and Times Square (1980) in centering women's experiences in punk and rock scenes. The screenplay by Cheri Lovedog draws from her own experiences as an LA musician, bringing authenticity to scenes of band dynamics, creative struggles, and the particular challenges faced by women in male-dominated spaces.

The film's exploration of aging in rock culture connects to documentaries like Bad Reputation (2018) about Joan Jett and L7: Pretend We're Dead (2016). These works challenge the youth-obsessed nature of rock while celebrating musicians who continue creating art on their own terms, regardless of commercial success or industry expectations.
